title: Didactic example — Central Limit Theorem in three plots
description: A realistic didactic walkthrough — three pre-rendered plots with prose between them, demonstrating how PlotImage carries an explanatory chapter that combines text and figures. NOTE: all three figures reuse the same gauss1d.png asset so the lesson renders even if higher-fidelity renders haven't been generated yet — the captions describe what each figure represents.

data.markdown:
## The Central Limit Theorem (CLT)

The CLT says: take a population with **any** distribution that has finite mean $\mu$ and finite variance $\sigma^{2}$. Draw $n$ independent samples and compute their mean $\bar{X}_{n}$. As $n$ grows, the distribution of $\bar{X}_{n}$ approaches a Gaussian centred on $\mu$ with standard deviation $\sigma / \sqrt{n}$ — *regardless of the shape of the original population*.

The three plots below illustrate the convergence: as $n$ grows from 1 to 30, the histogram of sample means morphs from the original (non-Gaussian) shape into something that is visually indistinguishable from a normal density.

:::callout{type="info" title="Why this matters"}
The CLT is the reason we can use $z$-tests, $t$-tests, and confidence intervals on sample means even when the underlying data is messy.
:::

data.alt: Sampling distribution of the mean at n=1 — looks like the original population
data.caption: Figure 1. At $n = 1$, the "mean of one sample" IS the sample, so the distribution is whatever the original population looks like (here, hypothetically a uniform draw on $[0, 1]$).
data.sourceCode:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=42)
samples = rng.uniform(0, 1, size=10_000)
plt.hist(samples, bins=40)
plt.title("Sampling distribution of the mean — n = 1")
plt.savefig("clt_n1.png")

data.markdown: Now repeat the experiment with $n = 5$ samples per mean. Each "observation" in the histogram below is the average of 5 uniform draws — and the distribution of those averages is already noticeably bell-shaped.

data.alt: Sampling distribution of the mean at n=5 — already concentrating
data.caption: Figure 2. At $n = 5$, the histogram concentrates around $\mu = 0.5$ and starts to look bell-shaped. The standard deviation has shrunk by a factor of $\sqrt{5}$.
data.sourceCode:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=42)
means = rng.uniform(0, 1, size=(10_000, 5)).mean(axis=1)
plt.hist(means, bins=40)
plt.title("Sampling distribution of the mean — n = 5")
plt.savefig("clt_n5.png")

data.markdown: By $n = 30$, the histogram is visually indistinguishable from a Gaussian — this is where the textbook rule-of-thumb "$n \geq 30$ is enough for the CLT" comes from. The rule depends on the original distribution's tails (heavy-tailed populations need more samples), but for benign shapes 30 is generous.

data.alt: Sampling distribution of the mean at n=30 — visually Gaussian
data.caption: Figure 3. At $n = 30$, the empirical histogram of sample means matches the theoretical Gaussian $\mathcal{N}\!\left(\mu = 0.5,\, \sigma^{2} = \tfrac{1/12}{30}\right)$ to within sampling noise.
data.sourceCode:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=42)
means = rng.uniform(0, 1, size=(10_000, 30)).mean(axis=1)
plt.hist(means, bins=40, density=True, alpha=0.7, label="empirical")

from scipy.stats import norm
x = np.linspace(0.3, 0.7, 400)
plt.plot(x, norm.pdf(x, loc=0.5, scale=np.sqrt((1/12) / 30)),
         color="red", label="theoretical Gaussian")
plt.legend()
plt.title("Sampling distribution of the mean — n = 30")
plt.savefig("clt_n30.png")
